chunks.text: Approved reference summary: RBI Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls, 2021. For payment workflows, assess strong authentication, fraud-risk management, secure application lifecycle, transaction reconciliation, logging, incident handling and relevant security testing. Confirm whether this direction or a more specific RBI direction applies to the regulated entity, payment channel, and third parties.

business objective: The system should provide a secure and standardized online loan application process that allows eligible customers to submit applications, upload required documents, undergo identity and credit verification, and receive an accurate approval or rejection decision. The main objective is to reduce manual processing, ensure consistent application of predefined lending rules, maintain complete audit trails, and support regulatory compliance.

The requirements and decision criteria should be clearly defined and approved before implementation so that each requirement can be systematically verified and validated users and roles: The main users are customers, loan officers, credit analysts, compliance officers, and system administrators. Customers should be able to create an application, enter required information, upload documents, and view the application status. Loan officers should review applications and verify submitted information. Credit analysts should evaluate creditworthiness and financial eligibility according to predefined criteria.

Compliance officers should verify regulatory requirements, audit records, and approve exceptions when required. System administrators should manage users, roles, configurations, and system access. Each role must have clearly defined permissions based on least privilege, and all important actions and decisions must be recorded for traceability and audit purposes. business rules: Loan decisions should be based on predefined and formally approved criteria. The main factors are credit score, repayment history, verified income, employment stability, debt-to-income ratio, requested loan amount, loan tenure, and existing financial obligations.

Each factor should have a predefined threshold and weighting factor. Applications that satisfy all mandatory eligibility criteria and achieve the minimum approved risk score can be approved. Applications that fail a mandatory criterion, fall below the minimum credit-score threshold, exceed the permitted debt-to-income ratio, or exceed the maximum eligible loan amount should be rejected. Borderline cases or applications requiring an exception should be routed to an authorized loan officer or credit analyst for manual review.

The scoring model, thresholds, and weighting factors must be documented, approved before implementation, and remain consistent unless a formally approved requirement change is made. exceptions: Loan approval criteria may be overridden only in formally defined exceptional cases, such as applicants with strong repayment history but temporary income variation, verified special circumstances, or cases requiring an approved policy exception. Overrides must not be allowed for mandatory regulatory, identity verification, or fraud-prevention requirements. Only authorized senior loan officers or credit managers should be permitted to approve an exception, based on predefined authority levels.

Every override must include the reason for the exception, the original decision and criterion that was overridden, supporting documents or evidence, the identity of the approving officer, date and time, and the final decision. All overrides must be recorded in an immutable audit trail and be available for compliance review and later verification. Changes to the override rules themselves must require formal approval and documentation.

security and compliance: The system must enforce role-based access control, least-privilege access, strong user authentication, encryption of sensitive data in transit and at rest, secure document storage, and complete audit logging of important user and decision-making activities. Customer identity must be verified using approved identity verification procedures before loan approval. Fraud detection should check for identity mismatches, duplicate applications, inconsistent information, suspicious documents, unusual application patterns, and other predefined fraud indicators.

Applications that trigger fraud or compliance rules must be automatically flagged and prevented from final approval until reviewed by an authorized officer. The system must comply with applicable financial, data-protection, KYC, and lending regulations. Security and compliance requirements must be explicitly documented and each requirement must have corresponding verification and validation tests before production deployment. validation and rollout: The system must be validated against the approved requirements before full rollout.

Validation should include unit testing of individual components, integration testing of interactions between services, system testing of the complete loan application workflow, security and compliance testing, and user acceptance testing by authorized loan officers and credit analysts. Test cases must be directly traceable to the corresponding requirements and predefined acceptance criteria. All mandatory functional, security, regulatory, and performance requirements must pass before deployment. Any failed test must be documented, corrected, and retested.

Formal stakeholder approval should be obtained after successful validation, followed by a controlled pilot deployment before full production rollout. service levels and scale: The system should support at least 20,000 loan applications per day and 2,000 concurrent users while maintaining reliable performance. Normal user interactions should respond within 2 seconds, while credit and risk analysis should complete within 10 seconds under normal operating conditions. The system should maintain at least 99.9% availability and provide automated backups and recovery mechanisms. The target recovery time objective should be 1 hour and the recovery point objective should be 15 minutes.

The system should scale horizontally as application volume increases without affecting the correctness of loan decisions or losing application, document, or audit data. These performance, availability, and recovery requirements must be formally specified and verified through predefined performance, load, stress, and recovery test cases before production deployment. data and integrations: The platform should integrate with internal customer, loan, document, credit assessment, risk scoring, and audit systems, as well as external identity verification services and credit bureau services.

Customer and application data should be exchanged using secure REST APIs with structured JSON formats, while documents should use approved secure document formats. Real-time API calls should be used for identity verification, credit checks, and risk assessment during application processing, while non-critical reporting and synchronization data can be exchanged periodically. All integrations must use encrypted communication such as HTTPS/TLS and authenticated service-to-service access. Incoming data must be validated for completeness, format, authenticity, consistency, and business-rule compliance before being accepted.

Failed or unavailable integrations should be logged, retried according to predefined rules, and the application should be placed on hold rather than proceeding with incomplete or unverified information. All integration requirements, data formats, validation rules, and security protocols must be formally documented and verified through integration test cases before deployment. workflow and outcomes: The workflow should follow a predefined and formally documented sequence. First, the customer selects a loan product and submits the application with the required personal, financial, and employment information.

The system validates the mandatory fields and documents before accepting the application. Next, identity and KYC verification are performed, followed by credit assessment, income verification, debt-to-income calculation, and risk scoring. The system then evaluates the application against the approved eligibility rules and decision thresholds. Applications that satisfy all mandatory criteria are automatically approved, while applications that fail mandatory criteria are rejected with a recorded reason. Borderline or exceptional applications are routed to an authorized loan officer or credit analyst for manual review.

Once approved, the customer receives the approval details and the loan proceeds to the final processing and disbursement stage. Every stage must produce a defined outcome and be recorded for traceability. Different loan products may have different approved eligibility criteria, limits, scoring thresholds, documentation requirements, and approval rules, but these variations must be explicitly defined and approved before implementation. delivery constraints: The rollout is subject to strict regulatory and compliance requirements, including KYC, data protection, lending regulations, auditability, and security controls.

Technical constraints include integration dependencies on credit bureaus, identity verification services, banking systems, and internal loan and risk systems, as well as requirements for high availability, secure data exchange, performance, scalability, and reliable recovery. Operational constraints include the need for trained loan officers and compliance personnel, controlled access to production systems, documented approval procedures, and support for manual review and exception handling. The system must also maintain complete traceability of requirements, decisions, configuration changes, and audit records.

These constraints and requirements should be formally defined and approved before implementation, with changes handled through a controlled change-management process and verified through appropriate testing before deployment.

factors.name: Requirement stability
factors.rationale: All requirements have an explicit approval status.

factors.name: Requirement clarity
factors.rationale: Measured from the presence of concrete, non-placeholder acceptance criteria.

factors.name: Risk
factors.rationale: Derived from stated high risk and security, privacy, regulatory, or audit classifications.

factors.name: Complexity
factors.rationale: Integration and data-management requirements increase coordination and technical complexity.

factors.name: Need for early prototype
factors.rationale: Unclear requirements or integration complexity make early learning and validation valuable.

factors.name: Time constraints
factors.rationale: No schedule or deadline evidence is available in the generated requirements; confirm this with the project sponsor.

factors.name: Customer involvement
factors.rationale: Derived only from business, stakeholder, or usability requirements; otherwise this must be confirmed.

factors.name: Frequency of changes
factors.rationale: Requirement documents do not establish the expected change rate; confirm with product and business stakeholders.

factors.name: Need for iterative development
factors.rationale: Unapproved or unclear requirements benefit from repeated review and validation cycles.

factors.name: Need for risk analysis
factors.rationale: Security/compliance concerns or complex integration warrant explicit risk analysis.

options.name: Waterfall
options.suitability: Best when requirements are stable, fully specified, and changes are controlled.

options.name: V-Shape
options.suitability: Best when each specification stage needs a linked verification and validation activity.

options.name: Spiral
options.suitability: Best when risk analysis, prototypes, and repeated risk-reduction cycles are central.

options.name: Prototyping
options.suitability: Best for validating uncertain user needs, workflows, and interfaces before committing to a full build.

options.name: Agile–V-Model hybrid
options.suitability: Best where evolving delivery needs formal verification and validation gates for regulated scope.

options.name: DevSecOps
options.suitability: Best where iterative delivery is paired with automated security, assurance, and operational controls.

options.name: Incremental
options.suitability: Best when value can be divided into validated, independently testable increments.

options.name: Agile
options.suitability: Best for frequent feedback and evolving requirements, with planned governance for high-risk work.

options.name: RAD
options.suitability: Best for time-boxed delivery with available users and modular, lower-risk scope.

sdlc.justification: Waterfall has the highest transparent score because requirement stability is baseline approved, requirement clarity is high, risk is high, complexity is high, need for early prototype is likely. Factors marked 'Not evidenced' are deliberately neutral and require stakeholder confirmation before the SDLC is approved.
